plan: Humanities passage (CLD-P-ACT-R-000048) on kintsugi; topic checked against every ACT Reading, SAT R&W, ACT English and ChatGPT verbal passage (no kintsugi passage). The origin legend is presented as a story that historians treat with caution. Ten questions, four aimed at hard (an author's mixed attitude, attributing positions in a debate, the purpose of a short supporting sentence, linking the conclusion to an earlier abstract claim). Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: Golden Joinery
passages.text:
Most methods of repairing a broken bowl aim at disappearance. A good glue line is a thin one; a skilled restorer fills chips and matches the glaze so that a visitor to a museum cannot tell where the object was damaged. The Japanese practice known as kintsugi, or "golden joinery," takes the opposite approach. The pieces are rejoined with lacquer, and the seams are then dusted or painted with powdered gold, so that the repair becomes the most conspicuous feature of the object.

A story often told about kintsugi's origin places it in the fifteenth century. According to the story, a Japanese military ruler sent a cracked tea bowl to China to be mended, and it came back held together with crude metal staples. Disappointed, Japanese craftsmen set out to find a repair that would be beautiful in its own right. Historians treat the story with caution; no document from the period records it, and lacquer had been used to mend ceramics in Japan long before. But the story persists, perhaps because it captures something true about the practice: kintsugi is a judgment about what a repair should look like, not merely a technique for making one.

The traditional method is slow. The lacquer, made from the sap of a tree, hardens only in warm, humid conditions, and each layer must cure for days before the next is applied. A single bowl may take weeks to restore. In recent years, kits sold online have promised "kintsugi in an afternoon," using quick-setting epoxy and gold-colored powder. Some practitioners object that these kits imitate the appearance of kintsugi while abandoning the patience that once made it meaningful. Others reply that the gold seam, not the lacquer, is what most people value, and that a cheaper method has simply brought the idea to more households.

Writers who admire kintsugi often describe it as a philosophy of embracing imperfection, and some go further, presenting it as a lesson for mending damaged relationships or recovering from personal loss. These comparisons are appealing, but they can obscure what the craft actually involves. A kintsugi repair does not pretend that the break never happened; neither does it celebrate breakage for its own sake. No restorer smashes a bowl in order to mend it. The practice values the object's whole history, including the accident, and asks the mender to make that history visible with care.

Perhaps that is why kintsugi bowls are rarely displayed as curiosities. In a tea room, a mended bowl is still used for tea. Its golden seams are not a sign that the bowl has been retired, but a record that someone thought it was worth keeping.

candidates.stem: Which of the following statements best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Kintsugi was invented in the fifteenth century after a Japanese tea bowl was poorly repaired in China.
choices.B: Kintsugi kits sold online have replaced the traditional method in most Japanese households.
choices.C: Kintsugi deliberately makes a repair visible, a choice whose meaning popular accounts can oversimplify.
choices.D: Kintsugi teaches that broken objects are more valuable than objects that have never been damaged.

candidates.evidence: kintsugi is a judgment about what a repair should look like
candidates.explanation: The passage contrasts kintsugi with invisible repair, examines its origin story and modern kits, cautions against oversimplified philosophical readings, and ends with the idea that the seams record that the bowl was worth keeping.

A.rationale: The passage says historians treat this origin story with caution.

B.rationale: The passage reports a debate about kits but makes no claim about how widely they have replaced the traditional method.

D.rationale: The passage says the practice does not celebrate breakage for its own sake.

hints: What does the author say kintsugi is, and what does the author caution against?
candidates.remember: A main idea should cover the author's central claim and qualifications.

candidates.stem: The first two sentences of the passage ("Most methods ... damaged") mainly serve to:

choices.A: present a usual goal of repair that kintsugi rejects.
choices.B: criticize museum restorers for hiding the history of damaged objects.
choices.C: explain the steps a museum restorer follows when matching the glaze of a broken bowl.
choices.D: argue that thin glue lines are stronger and longer lasting than thick glue lines.

candidates.explanation: The opening describes repairs that aim at disappearance; the passage then says kintsugi "takes the opposite approach."

B.rationale: The sentences describe invisible repair neutrally; they do not criticize restorers.

C.rationale: The sentences give the goal of invisible repair, not a set of steps.

D.rationale: The sentences concern visibility, not strength.

hints: What does the third sentence say kintsugi does?

strategy.explanation: Look at what comes right after the opening sentences.

candidates.remember: An opening description is often set up to be contrasted.

candidates.stem: Based on the passage, the author's view of the story about the stapled tea bowl is best described as:

choices.A: convinced that it accurately records how and when kintsugi first began in Japan.
choices.B: skeptical of its accuracy but appreciative of its point.
choices.C: dismissive of it as a popular story that misleads readers about what kintsugi is.
choices.D: uncertain whether kintsugi ever used lacquer before the fifteenth century.

candidates.evidence: But the story persists, perhaps because it captures something true about the practice
candidates.explanation: The author reports historians' caution about the story's accuracy but says it persists because it captures something true: kintsugi is a judgment about what a repair should look like.

A.rationale: The author notes that no document records the story and that lacquer repair existed earlier.

C.rationale: The author says the story "captures something true about the practice."

D.rationale: The author states that lacquer had been used to mend ceramics long before.

hints: Does the author accept the story as history? Does the author find it useless?

strategy.explanation: Read the sentences before and after "But the story persists."

candidates.remember: An author can doubt a story's facts while valuing its point.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must hold two attitudes at once; choices B and C each capture only half.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, the traditional kintsugi method is slow mainly because:

choices.A: the gold powder must be ground by hand from solid pieces of metal before each new repair.
choices.B: craftsmen must first study the history of each bowl before beginning a repair.
choices.C: the broken pieces must first be soaked in water for several weeks to remove any old glue.
choices.D: each layer of lacquer must cure for days before the next is applied.

candidates.evidence: each layer must cure for days before the next is applied
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the lacquer hardens only in warm, humid conditions and each layer must cure for days.

A.rationale: The passage does not say how the gold powder is made.

B.rationale: The passage does not describe such study as part of the method.

hints: Find the sentence after "The traditional method is slow."
candidates.remember: Detail questions are answered by a specific line.

candidates.subskill: Comparing two positions in a debate
candidates.stem: The defenders of kintsugi kits described in the third paragraph would most likely agree with which of the following statements?

choices.A: Most admirers care more about the gold seam than about the lacquer.
choices.B: The quick-setting epoxy in the kits is stronger than traditional lacquer.
choices.C: The traditional method's patience is what gives a kintsugi repair its meaning.
choices.D: Kits should be sold only to people who have studied the traditional method.

candidates.evidence: the gold seam, not the lacquer, is what most people value
candidates.explanation: The defenders reply that the gold seam, not the lacquer, is what most people value and that kits bring the idea to more households.

B.rationale: The defenders argue about what people value, not about strength.

C.rationale: This is the critics' view, not the defenders'.

D.rationale: Nothing suggests the defenders want to limit sales; they welcome wider access.

hints: Which group thinks patience is essential, and which does not?

strategy.explanation: Separate the critics' claim from the defenders' reply.

candidates.remember: When a passage presents two sides, keep track of which claim belongs to which side.

author_checklist.hardness: The critics' view is offered as a distractor; students must attribute each claim correctly.

candidates.stem: In the fourth paragraph, the statement "No restorer smashes a bowl in order to mend it" mainly serves to:

choices.A: show that kintsugi restorers are more careful than other restorers.
choices.B: support the claim that kintsugi does not celebrate breakage.
choices.C: suggest that the fifteenth-century origin story is unlikely to be true.
choices.D: explain why kintsugi bowls are rarely displayed as curiosities.

candidates.evidence: neither does it celebrate breakage for its own sake
candidates.explanation: The sentence follows the claim that kintsugi does not celebrate breakage for its own sake and supports it: breaking is never the goal.

A.rationale: The sentence is not a comparison of carefulness between restorers.

C.rationale: The sentence is in a paragraph about philosophical readings, not the origin story.

D.rationale: Display is discussed in the last paragraph, and this sentence is about breakage.

hints: What claim comes right before this sentence?

strategy.explanation: Connect the sentence to the claim it follows.

candidates.remember: A short, blunt sentence after a claim often serves as support.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must connect a brief example to the specific claim it supports rather than to nearby topics.

candidates.stem: As it is used in the first paragraph, the word "conspicuous" most nearly means:
candidates.evidence: so that the repair becomes the most conspicuous feature
candidates.explanation: The paragraph contrasts invisible repairs with kintsugi, which makes the repair the most "conspicuous," or noticeable, feature.

A.rationale: Gold is costly, but the sentence contrasts visible repair with invisible repair.

B.rationale: Nothing suggests the repair is fragile.

D.rationale: The word describes how the repair looks, not its history.

hints: What is the opposite of a repair that disappears?

strategy.explanation: Use the contrast with invisible repair.

candidates.remember: Use contrasts in the paragraph to define an unfamiliar word.

candidates.stem: The author suggests that comparing kintsugi to recovering from personal loss can be a problem because such comparisons:

choices.A: are never made by people who practice kintsugi themselves.
choices.B: encourage people to break objects so that they can repair them.
choices.C: are based on a mistranslation of the term "golden joinery."
choices.D: may hide what the craft actually involves.

candidates.evidence: but they can obscure what the craft actually involves
candidates.explanation: The author says these comparisons are appealing but can obscure what the craft actually involves.

A.rationale: The passage does not say who makes such comparisons.

B.rationale: The author says no restorer breaks a bowl to mend it, not that comparisons encourage breaking.

C.rationale: Nothing in the passage discusses translation.

hints: Find the sentence that begins "These comparisons are appealing."

strategy.explanation: Read the author's evaluation of the comparisons.

candidates.remember: Look for the author's own evaluative words, such as "but," after a description of others' views.

candidates.stem: According to the last paragraph, a mended kintsugi bowl in a tea room is typically:

choices.B: displayed behind glass as a curiosity.
choices.C: retired from use once it is repaired.
choices.D: sold to collectors who value the gold.

candidates.evidence: a mended bowl is still used for tea
candidates.explanation: The last paragraph says, "In a tea room, a mended bowl is still used for tea."

B.rationale: The passage says kintsugi bowls are rarely displayed as curiosities.

C.rationale: The passage says the seams are not a sign that the bowl has been retired.

hints: Find what happens to the bowl in a tea room.
candidates.remember: Answers to detail questions often repeat a phrase from the passage in other words.

candidates.subskill: Relationship between the conclusion and an earlier claim
candidates.stem: The last sentence of the passage most directly develops which earlier idea?

choices.A: A good glue line is a thin one, so that visitors cannot tell where an object was damaged.
choices.B: The lacquer hardens only in warm, humid conditions, and each layer must cure for days.
choices.C: The practice values the object's whole history, including the accident.
choices.D: A cheaper method has simply brought the idea of kintsugi to more households.

candidates.evidence: The practice values the object's whole history
candidates.explanation: The last sentence says the seams record that someone thought the bowl was worth keeping, which develops the idea that kintsugi values the object's whole history and makes it visible with care.

A.rationale: This describes the opposite approach, invisible repair, not the idea the last sentence develops.

B.rationale: This is a technical detail; the last sentence is about why the bowl is kept.

D.rationale: This is the defenders' argument about kits, not the idea the conclusion develops.

hints: What do the golden seams record, according to the last sentence?

strategy.explanation: Match the last sentence's idea to an earlier sentence.

candidates.remember: A conclusion often restates an earlier claim in concrete terms.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must link the closing image to an abstract claim two paragraphs earlier.
